title: Optimal sampling strategies in event-chain Monte Carlo
authors: James Gulliford, Gareth O. Roberts, Michael F. Faulkner
abstract: Event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) has revolutionised computational sampling over recent years, providing a powerful alternative to the molecular-dynamics (MD) and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithms. Each method outperforms the ubiquitous random-walk Metropolis algorithm by advancing particles along deterministic trajectories, but ECMC achieves this without being constrained by Newtonian dynamics. Recent advances exploited this dynamical freedom to induce a collective particle dynamics that relax local density variations on fast timescales. In a foundational model of $N$ pairwise-interacting particles on the 1D torus, this led to an $O(N^{3/4})$ improvement on the industry-leading computational efficiency of MD and HMC - but with an impractically small prefactor at low/high mean particle density for general attractive/repulsive interactions. Here we present a universal framework that generalises this high-efficiency sampling strategy to all translationally symmetric pairwise models on the torus - creating the potential to surpass MD and HMC as the state of the art. We also numerically elucidate the collective particle dynamics and discuss broad impact across the physical sciences and computational statistics.
summary: This paper presents a significant advancement in computational sampling by proposing the 'Cell-horizon ECMC' method for simulating interacting particles on a 1D torus. It rigorously compares this new strategy against existing methods, demonstrating superior computational efficiency and robustness across various particle densities. The work provides a powerful, general framework for simulating complex statistical mechanical systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop and compare optimal sampling strategies for Event-Chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) methods to surpass the computational efficiency of established algorithms like Molecular Dynamics (MD) and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC).
main_result: The authors introduce a universal framework, the 'Cell-horizon ECMC,' which achieves superior sampling efficiency, showing a better scaling and a higher mean event rate compared to non-factorised or standard-factorised ECMC methods.
method: The work involves deriving and comparing the mean event rates ($\Lambda$) and autocorrelation times ($	au_{mix}$) for various ECMC formulations, including non-factorised and cell-horizon approaches, using mathematical analysis of continuous-time Markov processes.
model_or_system: The primary model is $N$ pairwise-interacting particles confined to a 1D torus, governed by a potential $U$. Examples include the generalized harmonic chain (GHC) and the 1D soft-disk model (SD).
key_observables: Sampling efficiency, mean event rate ($\Lambda$), autocorrelation time ($	au_{mix}$), and the normalized pressure ($ eta P$).
important_parameters: Number of particles ($N$), inverse temperature ($ eta$), and the density ($ho$) of the system.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes translational symmetry for the pairwise potentials and relies on approximations when deriving the optimal cell-horizon rate.
figures_summary: Figure 8 compares the mixing times ($	au_{mix}$) for standard-factorised and optimal cell-horizon ECMC, showing $O(N^{5/2})$ vs $O(N^2)$ scaling for the GHC. Figure 7 confirms thermodynamic consistency by equating the normalized pressure ($ eta P$) with the ratio of index-space velocities ($v_{idx}/v_0$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first detailing existing ECMC strategies (non-factorised, standard-factorised), then introducing the novel cell-horizon framework, mathematically deriving its optimal rate, and finally comparing its performance and thermodynamic consistency against established methods.
why_interesting: The development of highly efficient, general sampling algorithms like this is crucial for simulating complex many-body systems in statistical mechanics, providing computational tools applicable to quantum many-body physics simulations.

FIG. 3. Comparative performance of cell-horizon ECMC against four-factor ECMC. (a) MC estimates of the computational effort Ω(defined in Section III) of both methods as a function of ρ at fixed N = 16 and at optimal b = b∗ P for both the p = 2 and p = 4 generalised harmonic chain ((βk)−1/p sets a lower length scale). For p = 2, results are consistent with Ωbeing insensitive to ρ (cell-horizon ECMC) and O(ρ−2) (four-factor ECMC). For p = 4, results are consistent with Ωbeing O(ρ−1) (cell-horizon ECMC) and O(ρ−4) (four-factor ECMC).
